item.title: The Daily Blogroll — Sunday, 30 August 2026
item.description:
Stargrace spots a Wurm Online rift in an absolutely awful mountainside location and keeps the verdict short: horrible.

Tipa shares how she’s using AI with EverQuest Legends logs, from vibe-coding a parser in Electron and TypeScript to ChatGPT-assisted build analysis.

Nimgimli argues it’s fine to drop games when sunk-cost guilt turns Steam-sale abundance and backlog management into homework.

Dávid rounds up Stargate-like games, especially Exogate Initiative’s base-management vibe and a charming unofficial Stargate point-and-click adventure.

Luna announces her giveaway winners and gives another cheerful shout for PancitoMerge and the story-rich delivery game Fading Serenades.

Welsh Troll says World of Tanks’ nonstop battle passes, mini-passes, events, and premium pressures have turned 16-year nostalgia into exhaustion.

Marc revisits Assault Suit Leynos, aka Target Earth, as an early Genesis standout that missed big sales but earned cult-classic longevity.

Wilhelm is glad Honest Game Trailers tackled Steam, from Half-Life 2-era digital distribution woes to sales, backlogs, Valve hardware, and early access.

Blockade85 gives Elite: Dangerous another real shot, finding slow progress through controls, docking, and Frame Shift frustration oddly rewarding.

Warner is deeply skeptical that Meta’s kid-safety settlement is anything more than a pricey PR move that still leaves Zuckerberg in control.

Jamie Zawinski is once again haunted by a mysteriously vanishing D key that only a Mac reboot or launching NoMachine seems to fix.

Dave Winer skips rude exit-popups, enjoys a beautiful Catskills day, and quietly pitches the nightly Scripting News email instead.

item.title: The Daily Blogroll — Saturday, 29 August 2026
item.description:
Frostilyte’s low-tier Pokémon Silver run heads toward Morty, detours through Sudowoodo and Togepi chores, and pauses to roast the Everstone.

Joel says Gris is a breathtaking watercolor platformer-puzzler, light on challenge but rich in atmosphere, music, and wordless emotional storytelling.

Margot talks backlog anxiety across Steam, Epic, PS5, and Switch, then highlights community projects that make actually playing those games feel doable.

Scopique breaks down Squadron 42’s delay to Q2 2027 and CIG’s attempts to steady Star Citizen after a rough 4.8 to 4.10 patch run.

Ellie revisits Marvel vs. Capcom as a slick, flashy 2D tag fighter that still lands, even if later sequels tend to steal its thunder.

Wilhelm and his daughter keep pushing Stardew Valley’s Community Center, upgrading the coop for a duck feather and making fishing easier with the cork bobber.

Michael rounds up a pile of obscure-game blog posts, celebrating everything from Gazillionaire to Journeyman Project 2 and inviting more people to join in.

Bruce Schneier’s weekly squid post spotlights Rhode Island’s very smelly ‘Squidpocalypse of ’26,’ featuring twenty tons of spilled squid.

Jimmy points readers to a new Analog Antiquarian post, a quick cross-link to his companion site’s latest historical essay.

Roger weighs IndieWeb ideals against the real cost and hassle of leaving Squarespace, framing self-hosting as possible but hardly painless.

Aywren compares blogging and YouTube, arguing video makes conversation easier while blogs still offer a more lasting home for thoughtful discussion.

Tipa wrestles with what it really means to belong to the IndieWeb, mixing practical membership steps with a candid, personal take on joining groups.

item.title: The Daily Blogroll — Friday, 28 August 2026
item.description:
Syp starts a brutal new RimWorld Naked Brutality run with Dismus, then celebrates a LOTRO carry-all making task-item clutter way less annoying.

Tipa dunks on Atari’s pricey Atari 2600 Activision rereleases, arguing River Raid nostalgia and some snazzy pins aren’t enough to justify the markup.

CrazyKinux expected Coriolis: The Great Dark exploration, but his group instead gets pulled into a murder mystery full of suspicious clues and funeral intrigue.

Azuriel turns a Sega Genesis memory lane trip into a love letter to Sonic 2, Blockbuster rentals, and Dune II blowing his mind.

Kimimi finds Dirge of Cerberus a weird but confident Final Fantasy VII shooter experiment, with Vincent Valentine fitting better than the stiff gunplay does.

Wilhelm uses EVE Online’s Exordium and its fully voiced tutorial to ask how long an MMORPG onboarding should be before it loses new players.

Anarchae rounds up privacy, security, and platform-power reads, with sharp notes on Google data ingestion, Steam’s dominance, and ID-scanning bars.

Ghastly revisits Summer Wars as a surprisingly current AI cautionary tale, with OZ’s internet dependency feeling uncomfortably close to today.

Tobold pushes back on Idiocracy doomposting, arguing the real story is widening educational inequality rather than one neat culprit like social media or AI.

Brennan turns blowing past Netlify’s free bandwidth into a candid post about self-hosting with Docker and Caddy, plus the personal cost of all that focus.

Owls has a rough time indiewebbing with microformats2, arguing its class-based semantics clash badly with Tailwind and feel less clean than HTML tags.

Tan checks in on a 2026 reading plan, balancing philosophy books, Greek classics, a buddy-read of Aristotle, and retro games stealing attention.

item.title: The Daily Blogroll — Thursday, 27 August 2026
item.description:
Cliffski’s nearly finished Ridiculous Space Battles challenge mode adds sortable lists, retaliation chains, and replays so players can actually study how they lost.

Bhagpuss’ grab-bag mostly turns into Ananta hype, with Gamescom finally delivering a January 2027 date for the anime-GTA open-world curiosity.

Krista rounds up easy Final Fantasy XIV fallback activities, from Gold Saucer and fishing to glamour, screenshots, and finally checking on Island Sanctuary.

Joar looks back on SWTOR’s killer eight-class-story hook and why the later shift to one shared narrative quietly broke its altoholic magic.

Sweetie explains how Persona 5 and Persona 3 Portable landed at the right moments, with youth, justice, and change giving the series lasting personal weight.

Wilhelm wraps Planet Crafter’s terraforming, then packs for a one-way hop to Selenea, where scarce iridium suddenly makes the moon trip feel precarious.

The Chronicler digs into Race to Berlin’s nasty two-player twist, where you race for Berlin while weaponizing the German armies against your rival.

The Friendly Necromancer gives Poetry Slammers more life with simple character animation, clearer Star Words, and suffix magnets for plurals and possessives.

Kelly reflects on retirement, mental health, and why blogging may provide the steady sense of purpose and accomplishment his brain still needs.

Aneesh jokes that Arch Linux might confer technical legitimacy, then credits Cat Hicks’ software-team psychology for helping him sidestep plenty of industry gatekeeping.

UltrViolet treats agentic AI like the next productivity tool and shares practical prompts for coding work in Claude Code and Google’s Antigravity IDE.

Juhis revisits Python parsing with BeautifulSoup, showing how HTML, XML, and handy CSS selectors can save a lot of scraping pain.

item.title: The Daily Blogroll — Wednesday, 26 August 2026
item.description:
Stargrace keeps WoW gold rolling across 10 servers, with rare greys and recipes selling nicely even while she barely plays beyond auction house duty.

Magi says Indiecator has now rejected 100 games over generative AI use, and lays out a blunt case against AI-made assets and tooling.

Wilhelm hits EverQuest Legends’ class lock-in, dumps paladin for wizard, eats the XP loss, and heads back into Blackburrow for offense.

Jamie Zawinski spots pricey 2013 Prince tickets on eBay and counters with a very Jamie pitch: support DNA Lounge and maybe get the real scraps.

Ramen Junkie says Cyberworld Scourge is a super simple Transformer, but the pirate-ship design and undead-looking details absolutely sell it.

Warner’s latest reading roundup ranges across gaslighting, history wars, forgotten photography, a 99-year-old fiddler, and a sharp Chekhov quote.

Joar wrestles with post-retirement consulting, where feeling flattered quickly gives way to fatigue and bigger questions about purpose after finance.

Tipa roasts Masters of the Universe for its joke-stuffed, not-really-Oklahoma He-Man movie setup, from Prince Adam to Skeletor and Dolph Lundgren.

Jeff’s UniFi 5G Backup test hits firmware loops, LTE-only AT&T service, and RedCap compatibility headaches in his mobile homelab build.

Dave Winer shares a new Frontier podcast, a handy tip for resuming Claude chats later, and a polite nudge toward the Scripting News email.

Cristian compares AliExpress pricing for an AMD Wraith Stealth cooler and finds a huge UK-versus-Romania gap, likely tied to geo-pricing, taxes, and shipping.

Blockade85 vents about covering another department’s calls with barely any training, then wisely decides tomorrow’s problem can wait until tomorrow.
